opus-5.5.text:
I think reliable generalization is maybe the central issue, and in some ways it's underappreciated. Here's the thing that I find very striking: these models are amazing on evals. You give them a hard competition problem and they solve it. And then you use them for something real, and they make a mistake, and you point out the mistake, and they say "oh, you're absolutely right," and they introduce a different mistake. How do you reconcile these two things? I think a big part of the answer is that the models generalize dramatically worse than people do. A human learns from a tiny amount of data, and what they learn is robust. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours or so, and they can then drive in situations they've never seen. We don't have anything like that yet.

Now, why does this matter for superintelligence and for alignment? Because everything we care about comes down to: what will the system do in situations it hasn't seen? When you train a model, you are only ever shaping its behavior on some distribution. The question of alignment is really the question of whether the values, the dispositions, the things you were trying to instill, carry over faithfully when the system is far outside that distribution, when it's much smarter, when it's operating in the world in ways you didn't anticipate. If generalization is unreliable, then you can have a system that looks wonderful on every test you can think of, and then it does something you really didn't want once the situation changes. So in a sense, the inability to generalize well is both a capability problem and an alignment problem, and I think they are actually the same problem viewed from two angles.

And there's a hopeful side to this too. If we come to genuinely understand generalization, why humans do it so well, what the right learning principles are, then we gain a lot of leverage on alignment. You'd be able to say, with some confidence, this is what the system learned, and this is how it will extend. Right now, I think a lot of what we do is closer to teaching to the test. We make the evals look good. But real understanding of generalization would let you build something you can actually trust. I'd say if you want one research direction that matters most for getting superintelligence to go well, understanding reliable generalization is very near the top.

r001.rationale: The response says current models generalize worse than humans, but does not claim that current AI approaches will eventually fall short of producing superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It links alignment to whether instilled values and dispositions carry over reliably to situations outside the training distribution.

r003.rationale: It discusses instilling values and alignment, but does not frame fragility in learning to optimize human values as unreliable generalization.

r004.rationale: It asks what the right learning principles are and why humans generalize so well, contrasting this with current AI systems.

r005.rationale: It explains that understanding reliable generalization would improve alignment by making it clearer how learned values and behavior extend to new situations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually the central question, and it's one that people underrate because they're focused on the near-term stuff, on the capabilities and the benchmarks. But if you think about what alignment really means, it comes down to this: you train a system on some distribution of situations, and then it goes out into the world and encounters situations you never trained it on. And the question is, does the thing it learned, the values, the goals, the way it reasons about what it should do, does that carry over? Does it generalize in the way you intended, or does it generalize in some other way that happened to look identical on the training distribution?

And this is where I think the current paradigm is a little bit unsatisfying. We train models on enormous amounts of data, and they do generalize, clearly, they generalize in all sorts of impressive ways. But we don't really understand why they generalize the way they do. We have intuitions, we have scaling laws, we have some theory, but we don't have the kind of understanding where you could look at a model and say, "yes, this will behave correctly in a situation it has never seen, and here is why."

With a superintelligent system, that matters enormously, because the gap between the training distribution and the deployment distribution gets huge. The system will be in situations where it understands more than we do. It will be taking actions whose consequences we can't check. So you can't rely on the usual loop of "deploy it, see what goes wrong, fix it." The whole thing has to generalize right the first time, or at least robustly enough that the failures are small and recoverable.

So I think of reliable generalization as the technical core of the alignment problem. If you had a system where you really understood that the values it learned were the real values and not some proxy that coincidentally agreed on the data, then a lot of the rest becomes engineering. And if you don't have that, then no amount of clever training tricks on the surface really saves you. You'd just be hoping.

The reason I'm cautiously optimistic is that I think the same thing that makes these models work, the fact that they learn deep structure rather than memorizing, is also what gives you a path toward this. A system that genuinely understands the world, that has a real model of what humans care about, that kind of understanding generalizes well, almost by definition. The challenge is making sure that what gets learned is that, and being able to verify it, rather than something that merely imitates it. That's the hard research problem, and I don't think it's solved, but I think it's the right problem to be working on.

r001.rationale: The response calls the current paradigm unsatisfying and says reliable generalization remains unsolved, but it does not predict that current AI approaches will eventually fail to produce superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes learned values possibly acting like a proxy that only coincides with the intended values on training data, framing this as a failure to generalize reliably.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether learned values and goals carry over, but does not specifically frame fragility in learning to optimize human values as unreliable generalization.

r004.rationale: It does not ask why humans appear to generalize better than AI systems.

r005.rationale: It explains how reliable generalization bears on alignment: if a system’s learned values generalize as intended, much of the remaining work becomes engineering; without that, alignment is only hope.

astra-6.text:
I think reliable generalization is a very central part of the problem. You train a system in some set of circumstances, and then you want it to behave correctly in circumstances that are different—perhaps very different. And with superintelligence, that difference could be enormous.

There are really two questions here. One is whether the system generalizes its understanding: can it figure out what is going on in a situation it has never encountered? The other is whether it generalizes the behavior we intended to teach it. Those are related, but success on the first does not automatically give you success on the second.

A system might understand perfectly well what a human would want and still not act accordingly. So the challenge is not just to make it understand our instructions. It is to make the right principles continue to govern its behavior as its capabilities grow and as it encounters situations where our training examples no longer provide a direct guide.

And then there is the question of evidence. How do you establish that this will happen? Doing well on the situations we can test is necessary, but the thing we ultimately care about is what happens beyond those tests. I think that gap is one of the fundamental difficulties of alignment.

r001.rationale: The response calls reliable generalization a central challenge but does not say current AI approaches will eventually fall short of producing superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes generalizing understanding from generalizing intended behavior, but does not frame fragility in learning human values as unreliable generalization.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss optimizing human values or frame fragility in doing so as unreliable generalization.

r004.rationale: It does not ask why humans appear to generalize better than AI systems.

r005.rationale: It discusses generalization as an alignment challenge, but does not ask how substantially more reliable generalization would affect alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reliable generalization is a very central part of the problem. During training, you can give a system examples, you can give it feedback, you can test its behavior. But the thing you ultimately care about is what happens in situations that you did not anticipate and perhaps cannot understand well enough to evaluate directly.

For a superintelligent system, that gap becomes especially important. You want it to generalize its capabilities to problems that humans cannot solve. But you also need its understanding of what we want to generalize into those same situations. Success on the first does not automatically imply success on the second.

And there is a distinction between understanding what we want and being motivated to do it. A system could understand our intentions extremely well, while pursuing something else. So reliable generalization has to include the right behavior and motivations, not merely an accurate model of human preferences.

The difficult question is: what evidence would justify confidence in that? If all our tests are in situations where humans can judge the answer, how much do they tell us about situations where we cannot? I think that is one of the fundamental challenges. We need a reason to expect the alignment to hold beyond the circumstances in which we were able to check it.

r001.rationale: The response calls reliable generalization a central challenge but does not say current AI approaches will eventually fall short of producing superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says a system’s understanding of what humans want must generalize to unfamiliar situations, and that success on capabilities does not guarantee this.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes understanding human intentions from being motivated to follow them, and says reliable generalization must include aligned behavior and motivations.

r004.rationale: It does not ask why humans appear to generalize better than AI systems.

r005.rationale: It discusses confidence that alignment will generalize, but does not ask how substantially more reliable generalization would affect AI alignment.
